case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts have jurisdiction to hear and grant relief on claims that DHS unlawfully obstructed noncitizens’ ability to seek asylum at or near the U.S. border, or whether those claims are barred by immigration jurisdiction-stripping provisions and border-entry doctrines.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily the Immigration and Nationality Act’s jurisdiction-limiting provisions (including 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and related limits tied to expedited removal), as applied to statutory asylum processing duties (8 U.S.C. § 1158) and constitutional constraints (Suspension Clause/Due Process) implicated by access-to-process claims.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (DHS and the Secretary) argue that challenges to border/asylum processing practices are effectively challenges to the removal system and thus fall within Congress’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252, leaving courts without authority to entertain broad, programmatic suits; they further contend that Supreme Court precedent such as DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms limited judicial review in the expedited-removal context and forecloses attempts to use habeas or similar mechanisms to expand review beyond what Congress authorized.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Al Otro Lado and allied plaintiffs) argue that their suit targets unlawful obstruction of access to the asylum process—i.e., failures to follow statutory and regulatory duties and unconstitutional interference with presenting at ports of entry—rather than a request to relitigate individual removal orders; accordingly, they contend § 1252 does not bar jurisdiction over systemic, pre-removal access-to-process claims and that Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it involved a post-entry individual’s habeas challenge to an expedited removal order, not organizational and classwide claims seeking prospective relief to ensure lawful access to asylum screening.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 579 U.S. 325 (2016) (cited for extraterritoriality framework; referenced at 136 S. Ct. 2090, 2101 (2016) in the excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to press Jennings’s warning against treating § 1252(b)(9) as an all-devouring zipper clause, and I can accept—without deciding the full scope of (b)(9)—that an “access-to-process” theory may be conceptually antecedent to any particular removal order. But even on that narrower path, the relief sought here is a systemwide, prospective injunction dictating how DHS conducts inspection and expedited-removal screening, and Justice Barrett’s structural point about § 1252(e)(3)’s specific, time-limited vehicle underscores that Congress did not authorize open-ended district-court management of that machinery. Justice Sotomayor’s rejoinder that § 1252(f)(1) is merely remedial does not overcome AADC’s treatment of (f)(1) as a jurisdictional limitation on lower courts’ power to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV in the programmatic way requested. Thuraissigiam, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, reinforces the minimalist and separation-of-powers concern that we should not permit relabeling to expand judicial supervision of expedited removal beyond the channels Congress prescribed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that these are antecedent “access-to-process” claims and Jennings warns against reading § 1252(b)(9) as an all-devouring zipper clause—does not overcome the separate, textually explicit limitation Congress enacted in § 1252(f)(1). As the Chief Justice explains, the relief sought is not merely adjudication of legality but a programmatic, prospective injunction that would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV’s inspection and expedited-removal machinery; AADC’s jurisdictional treatment of (f)(1) confirms lower courts lack power to issue that sort of systemic decree. Justice Barrett’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) further answers the “no forum” concern by showing Congress provided a specific, time-limited D.D.C. vehicle for systemic challenges, and Thuraissigiam reinforces that courts may not use alternative labels to expand review beyond Congress’s narrow channels in this context. Under an originalist and textualist approach, the best reading is to enforce the limits Congress wrote, even if respondents frame their claim as antecedent access rather than review of an order.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to warn—under Jennings—against treating § 1252(b)(9) as an all-devouring zipper clause and to frame this as an antecedent “access-to-process” claim, but that framing does not solve the remedial/jurisdictional obstacle in § 1252(f)(1). As the Chief Justice explains, the injunction respondents seek is not a narrow order to correct an isolated ultra vires act; it is programmatic, prospective supervision of inspection and expedited-removal operations, which “enjoin[s] or restrain[s] the operation” of Part IV and is therefore barred in the lower courts (with AADC supporting that (f)(1) functions as a jurisdictional limitation). Justice Barrett’s point about § 1252(e)(3) reinforces the structural inference that Congress provided a specific, time-limited vehicle for systemic challenges and did not authorize an open-ended district-court route by relabeling relief as “access.” Thuraissigiam does not answer every nuance, but it confirms we should not expand judicial involvement in expedited removal beyond Congress’s tightly drawn channels merely to avoid perceived accountability gaps.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s argument that § 1252(f)(1), read through AADC, bars the sort of programmatic, prospective injunction sought here is the strongest point from the petitioner side, and I accept it as a serious constraint on remedy. But I do not agree it resolves the antecedent jurisdictional question whether an ultra vires “access-to-process” claim—alleging officers are preventing noncitizens from invoking the inspection/asylum screening Congress mandated—falls within § 1252(b)(9) or § 1252(e) at all, especially under Jennings’s warning against treating (b)(9) as an all-devouring zipper clause. Justice Barrett’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) does not persuade me that Congress clearly created a no-forum zone for obstruction-of-process claims; that provision targets facial challenges to the expedited-removal system as designed, not allegations that officers are blocking entry into the statutory process in the first place. Consistent with the presumption of judicial review and practical consequences for vulnerable people at the border, I would keep the courthouse doors open to adjudicate legality while recognizing § 1252(f)(1) may require narrowing relief away from systemwide supervision toward more tailored, non-programmatic remedies.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on § 1252(f)(1) and AADC is the most serious obstacle, but I read it as primarily limiting the availability of classwide/programmatic injunctive relief rather than wiping out jurisdiction to adjudicate an ultra vires “access-to-process” claim in the first place—especially where the alleged misconduct prevents any statutory screening from occurring at all. Justice Barrett’s invocation of § 1252(e)(3) usefully shows Congress provided a channel for certain systemic challenges, yet that provision’s targeted, time-limited design does not clearly encompass claims that officers are refusing to initiate the very inspection/asylum process Congress mandated, and I am reluctant to infer a no-forum gap without clearer text. Thuraissigiam strengthens the caution against post-determination end-runs around Congress’s review limits, but it does not squarely answer whether antecedent obstruction claims “arise from” removal proceedings under § 1252(b)(9) or constitute “review” under § 1252(e) when no determination exists. On a pragmatic textualist view, the workable middle ground is to keep a forum open to decide legality while narrowing relief to avoid the (f)(1) concern rather than dismissing outright.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to invoke Jennings’s caution against reading § 1252(b)(9) as an all-devouring “zipper clause,” and I’m prepared to assume (without deciding) that an antecedent “access-to-process” claim might fall outside (b)(9). But Chief Justice Roberts’s point about § 1252(f)(1) remains dispositive for this case as pleaded: respondents’ requested systemic, prospective injunction would necessarily “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV by judicially supervising frontline inspection and expedited-removal screening, relief Congress barred lower courts from issuing (AADC’s jurisdictional treatment strengthens that conclusion). Justice Barrett’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) further undercuts the asserted “accountability vacuum” by showing Congress specified a narrow, time-limited mechanism for programmatic challenges, making it improper for us to create an open-ended district-court workaround. Thuraissigiam reinforces the same separation-of-powers lesson: courts may not expand remedies in this domain by relabeling process disputes, even when the equities feel weighty.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the strongest respondent point: under Jennings we should not read § 1252(b)(9) as an all-devouring zipper clause that creates a no-forum vacuum for antecedent “access-to-process” claims. But even accepting that narrowing, Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on § 1252(f)(1) remains dispositive for this case because the relief requested is a systemic, prospective injunction that would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, which AADC treats as a jurisdictional bar on lower-court injunctions of this sort. Justice Barrett’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) further undercuts the vacuum premise by showing Congress provided a specific, time-limited D.D.C. mechanism for systemic challenges, implying it did not authorize open-ended nationwide district-court supervision of border screening. Under my institutionalist, text-and-structure approach (and consistent with Thuraissigiam’s caution against relabeling to expand review in expedited-removal settings), I would reverse without deciding the outer limits of (b)(9) because (f)(1) blocks the remedy sought here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Jennings cautions against reading § 1252(b)(9) as an all-devouring “zipper clause,” and that an antecedent “access-to-process” claim risks falling into an accountability gap—does not, in my view, overcome the distinct textual barrier of § 1252(f)(1) given the remedy respondents actually seek. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes (echoing AADC’s treatment), a systemwide, prospective injunction that would supervise and reshape frontline inspection/expedited-removal screening would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, which (f)(1) forbids lower courts to do; even if jurisdiction to adjudicate some narrow legality question exists, this particular form of relief is not available. The statutory structure also cuts against the “no forum” premise: § 1252(e)(3) provides a specific, time-limited vehicle for systemic challenges in D.D.C., suggesting Congress anticipated and tightly cabined programmatic litigation rather than inviting open-ended nationwide district-court supervision. Thuraissigiam reinforces the methodological caution against repackaging demands for additional front-end process to expand review beyond the channels Congress expressly allowed in the expedited-removal context.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s point that § 1252(f)(1), reinforced by AADC, bars lower courts from issuing sweeping, programmatic injunctions is the most serious obstacle, and I agree it likely requires substantial narrowing of any forward-looking relief. But I do not read (f)(1) to answer the antecedent question pressed by Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor: whether §§ 1252(b)(9) and 1252(e) clearly strip jurisdiction over an ultra vires “access-to-process” claim alleging officers are preventing initiation of the very statutory screening Congress mandated. Justice Barrett’s reliance on § 1252(e)(3) shows Congress provided one avenue for certain systemic challenges, yet it is not a clear statement that all other legality claims about threshold obstruction are jurisdictionally barred—especially where the alleged misconduct prevents any proceedings from occurring at all. On my procedural-fairness, pragmatic view and the presumption of judicial review, I would treat § 1252(f)(1) as principally a remedial constraint (pushing toward individual-focused, non-programmatic relief), not a wholesale courthouse-closure that would, in practical consequence, insulate front-end obstruction from meaningful judicial checking.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress in IIRIRA erected a comprehensive channeling scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 designed to prevent broad, programmatic litigation from interfering with the removal system, and we should respect that unmistakable legislative choice in light of institutional concerns and federalism. As Thuraissigiam emphasizes, IIRIRA’s “theme” is protecting Executive discretion and limiting judicial review in the expedited-removal context, making it difficult to recast challenges to border/asylum processing as freestanding “access-to-process” claims outside § 1252. Even if some claims are not direct challenges to particular removal orders, § 1252(f)(1) at minimum curtails lower courts’ authority to issue classwide or programmatic injunctions “enjoin[ing] or restrain[ing] the operation” of Part IV, and AADC characterizes § 1252(f)(1) as a jurisdictional limit on such injunctive relief. A narrower disposition would therefore hold that the requested systemic relief is barred (and that any review must proceed, if at all, through Congress’s specified avenues), without opining broadly on the merits of DHS’s policies.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and limits judicial review of claims “arising from” removal proceedings and specific enforcement decisions, and § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(g) foreclose broad, programmatic suits that effectively challenge how DHS administers the admission/removal system rather than a discrete, reviewable final order. As Thuraissigiam confirms, noncitizens at the threshold (including those apprehended shortly after unlawful entry or presenting at a port) possess only the process Congress has provided, and courts may not use habeas or equitable relief to enlarge review beyond what § 1252 authorizes. Even if framed as “access-to-process” claims under § 1158, the relief sought would intrude on Congress’s chosen review scheme for expedited removal and admission determinations, where § 1252(e) sharply limits review. Given the Constitution’s allocation of immigration and admission control to the political branches and the statute’s jurisdiction-stripping language, federal courts lack jurisdiction here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping scheme in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 is written broadly to preclude district-court jurisdiction over claims that in substance “arise from” the expedited-removal and admission system, and § 1252(e)(1) specifically bars classwide/systemic challenges outside the narrow habeas review Congress allowed in § 1252(e)(2). Even if styled as “access-to-process” claims, respondents’ requested prospective relief would necessarily “enjoin or restrain the operation” of the expedited-removal/admission framework and thus runs headlong into Congress’s limits, including § 1252(f)(1) and the carefully cabined review provisions. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that, in the expedited-removal context, Congress may sharply limit judicial review and courts should not expand review via habeas-like or programmatic suits beyond what § 1252 authorizes. Given the statutory text and the practical consequences for border administration and law enforcement, federal courts lack jurisdiction to entertain these broad challenges outside the channels Congress prescribed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(9) channels only those claims that “arise from” removal proceedings, and under this Court’s narrowing constructions in cases like Jennings v. Rodriguez it should not be read as a “zipper clause” that swallows all challenges merely related to immigration enforcement. Respondents’ suit targets DHS’s alleged systemic obstruction of access to the statutory asylum process (8 U.S.C. § 1158) at or near ports of entry, seeking prospective relief to ensure lawful screening, rather than review of any individual removal order or the validity of expedited-removal determinations—making § 1252’s jurisdiction-stripping provisions a poor fit. DHS v. Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it involved a post-entry individual habeas challenge to an expedited removal order and Congress’s limits on that narrow form of review under § 1252(e), not a pre-removal, access-to-process claim alleging the agency is preventing people from invoking the very procedures Congress mandated. Reading § 1252 to foreclose jurisdiction over such access claims would risk leaving vulnerable asylum seekers without any meaningful forum to remedy ongoing unlawful practices, contrary to basic fairness and the presumption that Congress does not lightly close the courthouse doors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252’s channeling scheme is textually aimed at review of removal orders and decisions made “in” removal proceedings, and § 1252(e)(3) provides an exclusive D.D.C. forum only for systemic challenges to the “validity” of the expedited-removal “system” and its implementing regulations/policies—not for claims that officers at ports of entry are unlawfully refusing to perform the distinct, mandatory inspection/asylum-processing duties Congress set out in 8 U.S.C. §§ 1158(a)(1) and 1225. Reading § 1252 to bar all pre-removal, access-to-process suits would create a serious workability and coherence problem by insulating alleged agency noncompliance with those statutory commands from any meaningful judicial check, contrary to the strong presumption favoring judicial review of unlawful agency action. DHS v. Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it involved an individual post-entry habeas challenge seeking expanded review of an expedited-removal order, whereas respondents seek prospective relief to prevent obstruction of access to the statutory asylum process at or near ports of entry. On this narrower understanding, the federal courts retain § 1331/APA-type jurisdiction at least to adjudicate whether DHS is acting ultra vires in a way that prevents noncitizens from invoking § 1158(a)(1)’s “irrespective of status” right to apply for asylum.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and sharply limits judicial review over claims arising from inspection and expedited-removal processes, and § 1252(e) in particular confines review to narrow identity/status questions, leaving little room for broad, programmatic challenges seeking systemic injunctions at or near the border. Read in light of § 1252(a)(2)’s jurisdiction-stripping and channeling design, respondents’ access-to-process theory still “arises from” and would effectively restructure the very admission/removal screening scheme Congress placed largely beyond district-court supervision. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that, for expedited-removal-related claims, Congress may restrict review to the statutory minimum and that courts should not expand review through habeas-like or APA framing to obtain relief beyond what § 1252 authorizes. Whatever the equities, the separation of powers requires courts to respect the limits Congress imposed, leaving these claims to the administrative process and the specific judicial review mechanisms Congress provided.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Congress in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 built a tightly reticulated scheme channeling and limiting judicial review of claims arising from inspection, admission, and expedited removal, and § 1252(e)(1)–(2) in particular restricts courts’ ability to entertain suits that would effectively expand review beyond what Congress authorized. Although respondents frame their case as a pre-removal, systemic “access-to-process” challenge, the requested prospective relief would in practical effect regulate and supervise DHS’s front-end admission and expedited-removal machinery, the very area where § 1252’s jurisdictional limits are strongest. Our decision in DHS v. Thuraissigiam underscores that, especially in the expedited-removal context, courts may not use habeas-like or equitable vehicles to obtain broader process or review than Congress has provided, and that principle applies with equal force to programmatic suits that would circumvent the statutory channeling rules. Given precedent, history at the border, and the workability/legitimacy concerns of inviting nationwide structural injunctions in this domain, I would hold the claims largely jurisdiction-barred (absent a clearly preserved, narrow constitutional exception not shown here).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252 reflects Congress’s choice to channel and sharply limit judicial review of claims “arising from” the inspection, expedited-removal, and removal processes, and provisions like § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(e) are naturally read to preclude broad, programmatic district-court suits that would effectively supervise how DHS implements border screening and expedited removal. Respondents’ requested systemic, prospective relief would function as indirect review of expedited-removal/asylum-screening administration outside the exclusive review pathways Congress specified, and § 1252(e)(3) in particular indicates that facial or systemic legality challenges to expedited-removal procedures must proceed only in the manner, forum, and timing Congress authorized. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that, in this context, the Suspension Clause does not require courts to provide review beyond what Congress has provided for expedited removal, undermining efforts to repackage barred review as “access-to-process” claims. While some claims about obstruction at ports of entry may feel antecedent to a removal order, § 1252’s broad channeling language and the statutory structure favor treating these challenges as part of the removal system that Congress committed to limited review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The plaintiffs’ claims are best understood as pre-removal, access-to-process challenges to DHS’s alleged obstruction of the statutory opportunity to apply for asylum under 8 U.S.C. § 1158, not as collateral attacks on individual removal orders, and thus fall outside § 1252’s most stringent jurisdiction-channeling rules tied to “review” of removal orders and expedited-removal determinations. While § 1252(e) sharply limits review in the expedited-removal context, it is directed at constraining case-by-case and order-focused review, and it does not clearly and unequivocally strip courts of jurisdiction over systemic prospective claims that officials are unlawfully preventing noncitizens from invoking the asylum screening framework in the first place—especially where procedural fairness and meaningful access to statutorily required process are at stake. DHS v. Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it involved a post-entry individual’s habeas challenge seeking additional review of an expedited removal order, whereas respondents seek forward-looking relief to ensure access to the initial asylum process rather than expanded merits review of removal outcomes. Absent a clearer statement that Congress meant to foreclose all judicial forums for such access-to-process claims, I would not extend § 1252 to bar jurisdiction where the practical consequence would be insulating potentially unlawful obstruction of statutory and constitutional process from any meaningful judicial check.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts have jurisdiction to hear APA and constitutional claims challenging DHS policies and practices that allegedly block or frustrate noncitizens’ ability to seek asylum at or near the U.S. border, or whether those claims are barred by immigration-channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions and limited by the nature of habeas review.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily 8 U.S.C. § 1252 (including subsections that channel review to petitions for review and limit district-court jurisdiction), as applied to challenges implicating asylum processing at/near the border, alongside the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. §§ 701–706) and (to the extent constitutional limits are argued) the Suspension Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 2) and Due Process principles.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (DHS and the Secretary) contend that respondents’ suit is an impermissible attempt to obtain district-court review of immigration enforcement and removal-related decisions and procedures that Congress has routed into the INA’s exclusive review scheme; they argue that 8 U.S.C. § 1252 forecloses jurisdiction over these claims (including systemwide or programmatic challenges tied to processing and removal), that respondents cannot use the APA to evade Congress’s channeling limits, and that Supreme Court precedent—particularly DHS v. Thuraissigiam—confirms that noncitizens at the threshold (or recently apprehended) have sharply limited avenues for judicial review beyond the narrow scope Congress provided.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Al Otro Lado and others) argue that they are not seeking forbidden review of individual removal orders but instead are challenging unlawful DHS policies/practices that obstruct access to the asylum process (e.g., turning away or misdirecting asylum seekers, or otherwise preventing them from applying), making their claims classic APA and constitutional challenges to agency action; they maintain that § 1252’s jurisdictional bars do not reach these access-to-process claims (or, if read that broadly, would raise serious constitutional concerns), and that Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it addressed the limited scope of habeas to attack an expedited removal order—whereas respondents seek prospective relief to ensure access to statutory asylum procedures rather than release from custody or invalidation of a specific removal order.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 579 U.S. 325 (2016) (cited for extraterritoriality principles, as referenced in the provided excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the strongest point that, under Jennings, § 1252(b)(9) should not be treated as a universal “zipper clause,” and that these are upstream access-to-process claims that might never generate an order or record for review. But even granting that limitation on (b)(9), the relief sought here necessarily entails ongoing district-court supervision of DHS’s § 1225(b)(1) expedited-removal screening “procedures,” and Justice Gorsuch is right that § 1252(a)(2)(A) is unusually targeted and emphatic in foreclosing jurisdiction over claims arising from those very determinations and procedures. Justice Sotomayor’s “no forum” concern is serious, yet under a minimalist, precedent-respecting approach I cannot use constitutional-avoidance pressure to narrow clear jurisdiction-stripping text, particularly in light of Thuraissigiam’s reinforcement that Congress may tightly confine review for threshold entrants. I would therefore hold narrowly that district-court jurisdiction is barred for these programmatic APA claims and this kind of systemic injunction, without resolving what narrower, order-tethered routes might remain within the INA scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson’s best point is the Jennings caution against reading § 1252(b)(9) as a universal “zipper clause,” coupled with the asserted “no forum” consequence for upstream access-to-process claims. But even if (b)(9) has limits, Justice Gorsuch rightly emphasizes that § 1252(a)(2)(A) is a targeted, unusually emphatic preclusion of jurisdiction over any cause or claim “arising from” § 1225(b)(1) “procedures” and “determinations,” which squarely describes respondents’ attempt to obtain programmatic APA supervision of border-screening machinery. Under an originalist and textualist approach, the perceived harshness of a “no forum” result cannot justify narrowing Congress’s clear jurisdiction-stripping text, and Thuraissigiam reinforces that for threshold entrants Congress may confine review to the narrow avenues it specified rather than courts creating alternative fora. I therefore remain with the Petitioner and would not extend Jennings to override the specific bar Congress enacted in (a)(2)(A).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right to invoke Jennings’s warning against treating § 1252(b)(9) as a universal “zipper clause,” and their “upstream access-to-process” framing is the best way to try to avoid channeling. But even assuming (b)(9) does not reach every such claim, § 1252(a)(2)(A) is the more targeted and unusually emphatic bar here: respondents seek an APA-based, programmatic injunction that would necessarily supervise the § 1225(b)(1) expedited-removal screening “procedures” and related “determinations,” exactly what Congress said courts may not review. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch stress, the APA cannot supply jurisdiction Congress has withdrawn, and Thuraissigiam reinforces that for threshold entrants Congress may confine review to the narrow avenues it provided rather than invite district-court oversight of border-processing machinery. The “no forum” concern flagged by Justice Sotomayor does not permit us to narrow clear jurisdiction-stripping text via constitutional-avoidance when the requested relief would functionally circumvent the statutory design.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point head-on: § 1252(a)(2)(A)’s references to “procedures” and “determinations” under § 1225(b)(1) are unusually emphatic, and courts must not use the APA to recreate jurisdiction Congress has withdrawn. But as Justice Kagan stresses via Jennings, we should not treat the channeling provisions as a universal zipper where the practical effect is to erase any forum for claims that the Government is preventing the statutory asylum mechanism from ever being invoked in the first place—before an order, record, or “order-tethered” pathway can exist. Thuraissigiam, invoked by Justice Thomas and Justice Alito, powerfully confirms Congress’s ability to narrow review of an existing expedited-removal order for threshold entrants, yet it does not clearly answer whether Congress also foreclosed all prospective judicial review when the alleged illegality is upstream obstruction of congressionally mandated access-to-process. Under my pragmatic approach, absent unmistakably clear text eliminating all review of such access claims, I would avoid reading § 1252 to immunize systemic statutory noncompliance that disproportionately harms the most vulnerable.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that the requested injunction would look like district-court supervision of § 1225(b)(1) “procedures,” and § 1252(a)(2)(A) speaks unusually broadly to foreclose review of those determinations and procedures. But I do not think that breadth can be read to extinguish jurisdiction over a narrowly framed claim that the Government is preventing the statutory asylum process from ever commencing, because Jennings—invoked by Justice Jackson as well—rejects construing § 1252(b)(9) as a universal “zipper clause” that sweeps in upstream, non–order-tethered claims. Thuraissigiam, emphasized by Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh, confirms Congress may sharply limit review of an existing expedited-removal order for threshold entrants; it does not clearly answer whether Congress also eliminated any judicial forum for prospective compliance-with-statute claims not seeking to review, set aside, or stay any order. Under a pragmatic textualism, I would read § 1252 to bar programmatic restructuring of expedited-removal screening while still permitting carefully limited relief aimed at access to the congressionally created process—otherwise we risk an overinclusive construction that collapses Jennings’s limiting principle and creates serious no-forum problems without a clear statement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson raise the strongest counterpoint: Jennings cautions that § 1252(b)(9) is not a universal “zipper clause,” and an upstream access-to-process claim may never generate a reviewable order. But even granting that limitation on (b)(9), § 1252(a)(2)(A) independently and pointedly strips jurisdiction over “any…cause or claim” arising from § 1225(b)(1) “procedures” and “determinations,” and the requested systemwide injunction would necessarily entail judicial supervision of that very machinery, as the Chief explains. Justice Sotomayor’s “no forum” and constitutional-avoidance concerns cannot justify narrowing what Congress wrote with the “unusually emphatic” clarity Justice Roberts identifies, especially in light of Thuraissigiam’s reinforcement (as Justice Thomas notes) that threshold entrants may be confined to the limited review Congress specified. On a textualist/originalist account of separation of powers, the APA cannot supply an alternative district-court forum where Congress has expressly precluded it; the remaining question is only what INA-provided channels, if any, remain for narrower, order-tethered claims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right to invoke Jennings’s warning against reading § 1252(b)(9) as a universal “zipper clause,” and their “no forum” concern is the strongest point on the other side. But even if (b)(9) has limits, Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch correctly emphasize that § 1252(a)(2)(A) is a targeted, unusually emphatic bar on jurisdiction over claims arising from § 1225(b)(1) “procedures” and “determinations,” and the requested systemwide injunction would necessarily entail district-court supervision of that border-screening machinery. Under an institutionalist, text-and-precedent approach, Thuraissigiam reinforces Congress’s authority to confine threshold-entrant review to the narrow channels it specified, and the APA cannot reopen district-court jurisdiction where Congress precluded it. I would therefore hold narrowly that district-court jurisdiction is barred for these claims and this form of programmatic relief, without foreclosing whatever INA-specified, order-tethered avenues might remain in other postures.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the best counterpoint: under Jennings, § 1252(b)(9) is not a universal “zipper clause,” and an upstream access-to-process claim might otherwise lack any order-tethered forum. But even granting Jennings’s limiting principle on (b)(9), I find Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s focus on § 1252(a)(2)(A) dispositive: Congress specifically barred jurisdiction over any claim arising from § 1225(b)(1) “procedures” and “determinations,” and the systemwide injunction sought would require ongoing judicial supervision of that very machinery. Justice Sotomayor’s no-forum and constitutional-avoidance concerns do not justify narrowing unusually explicit jurisdiction-stripping text, and Thuraissigiam reinforces that Congress may confine review for threshold entrants to the limited avenues it provided rather than allow an APA programmatic end-run. On a textualist/originalist reading, the better view is that district-court jurisdiction is precluded for these claims and this form of relief, even if narrower INA-specified review might exist in other postures.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest textual point: § 1252(a)(2)(A) is unusually specific in barring review of § 1225(b)(1) “procedures” and “determinations,” and the requested injunction could look like ongoing judicial management of DHS screening. But under Jennings (as Justice Kagan emphasizes), I am not persuaded Congress clearly used that language to eliminate any forum for claims that the Executive is categorically preventing the statutorily required process from ever initiating—an upstream access-to-process allegation that may never produce an order, record, or viable petition-for-review route. Thuraissigiam reinforces Congress’s power to limit review of an existing expedited-removal order for threshold entrants, yet it does not squarely resolve whether Congress also foreclosed prospective suits aimed at ensuring the government follows Congress’s own procedural predicates before an order exists. Pragmatically and consistent with procedural fairness, I would read § 1252 to bar order-review and programmatic merits relitigation, but not to immunize alleged systemic obstruction of congressionally mandated access to process where no alternative channel realistically exists.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252’s channeling provisions—particularly § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(a)(2)—reflect Congress’s choice to route challenges that arise from DHS’s inspection, processing, and removal machinery into the INA’s exclusive review scheme rather than broad district-court APA suits, and respondents’ requested systemwide injunction would effectively supervise those removal-related procedures. Under DHS v. Thuraissigiam, noncitizens at the threshold (or in expedited-removal contexts) have sharply limited judicial review, and they cannot use the APA to obtain broader merits review than Congress allowed through § 1252(e)(2)’s narrow habeas-like inquiries. Whatever the merits of respondents’ access-to-asylum allegations, a narrow, institutionally cautious disposition would hold that district-court jurisdiction is barred and that any review must proceed, if at all, through the channels Congress specified. This reading also avoids expanding constitutional habeas beyond the limited historical core recognized in Thuraissigiam while respecting Congress’s federalism- and separation-of-powers-driven jurisdictional design in § 1252.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252 channels and restricts judicial review of claims that arise from or are intertwined with the inspection, expedited-removal, and related admission/removal processes, and it does so through an exclusive review scheme that precludes end-runs via the APA. Respondents’ “access-to-process” challenges are, in substance, programmatic attacks on DHS’s border-processing and removal-related practices and thus fall within § 1252’s jurisdiction-stripping provisions rather than ordinary district-court APA review. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that for noncitizens at or just across the threshold, Congress may sharply limit judicial review and that habeas, at minimum, does not constitutionally guarantee the broader prospective relief respondents seek beyond the narrow review Congress provided. Reading § 1252 according to its original public meaning and enacted text, federal courts lack jurisdiction here, and any contrary precedent should yield to the statute’s clear channeling command.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and restricts judicial review of claims “arising from” the inspection, removal, or expedited-removal process, and respondents’ programmatic challenge to border screening and asylum processing is tightly intertwined with those removal-related determinations, bringing it within 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(a)(5), and likely within § 1252(g) to the extent it targets the Executive’s initiation/processing of removal. Respondents cannot use the APA to evade Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping scheme, since the APA does not confer jurisdiction and yields where statutes preclude review. Thuraissigiam confirms that for recent/arriving noncitizens at the threshold, Congress may sharply limit judicial review to what it has provided, and broad district-court suits seeking systemic relief would circumvent that scheme. Although Jennings cautions against reading § 1252(b)(9) as swallowing all claims, this suit is not meaningfully “collateral” to removal; it challenges the very machinery of border processing that Congress placed within the INA’s exclusive review framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Respondents’ claims target DHS policies and practices that allegedly prevent noncitizens from accessing the asylum process at all—i.e., they challenge a barrier to initiating the statutory scheme under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1) and DHS’s inspection/processing duties under § 1225—rather than seeking review of any individual expedited removal order. Read in context, 8 U.S.C. § 1252’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping provisions are aimed at routing review of removal orders and proceedings into petitions for review and limiting collateral attacks; they should not be extended to foreclose all prospective APA claims (5 U.S.C. §§ 701–706) where the alleged illegality is upstream of, and effectively prevents, any administrative record or reviewable order from ever existing. DHS v. Thuraissigiam addressed the narrow scope of habeas to set aside an expedited removal order and does not compel denying district-court jurisdiction over forward-looking access-to-process challenges that seek to ensure the government follows Congress’s asylum framework rather than secure release or overturn a particular order. Construing § 1252 to preclude any judicial forum for such claims would raise serious constitutional concerns, including under the Suspension Clause and basic due process principles, especially given the real-world impact on vulnerable asylum seekers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252’s channeling provisions—especially § 1252(b)(9) and § 1252(g)—should not be read to swallow all APA and constitutional challenges that are not seeking review of a removal order or the conduct of a removal proceeding, but instead allege that DHS has adopted policies/practices that prevent noncitizens from ever accessing the statutory asylum process in the first place. As construed in Jennings v. Rodriguez, § 1252(b)(9) is not a “zipper clause” for every claim that has some factual connection to immigration enforcement; and Nielsen v. Preap likewise cautions against overexpansive “arising from” readings that would sweep in claims Congress did not clearly route into the petition-for-review scheme. DHS v. Thuraissigiam is distinguishable because it addressed the limited scope of habeas to attack an expedited removal order, whereas respondents seek prospective, process-access relief that does not require a court to review or invalidate any specific removal order. Reading § 1252 to bar any forum for such access-to-process claims would create serious constitutional-avoidance concerns, so the better textual and workable interpretation is that district courts retain jurisdiction over these non-order, non-habeas APA/constitutional challenges.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and restricts judicial review for claims that are, in substance, attempts to contest the manner in which DHS executes admission, expedited removal, and related screening at the border; § 1252(b)(9) consolidates review of all questions of law and fact “arising from” actions taken to remove a noncitizen into the petition-for-review scheme, and § 1252(a)(2)(A) sharply limits judicial review of determinations and procedures under § 1225(b)(1). Respondents’ APA framing cannot override Congress’s jurisdictional design, because the APA does not create jurisdiction and yields where statutes “preclude judicial review,” 5 U.S.C. § 701(a), and here Congress has spoken with unusual clarity. Reading these provisions according to their ordinary meaning, and mindful of separation-of-powers limits on judicial revision of a comprehensive immigration review scheme, the district courts lack jurisdiction over these systemwide challenges insofar as they target border-processing and expedited-removal-related practices. DHS v. Thuraissigiam reinforces that, for threshold entrants subjected to expedited removal, Congress may confine judicial review to the narrow avenues it provided and habeas cannot be expanded into broader merits review of the government’s screening process.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Congress in 8 U.S.C. § 1252 created a comprehensive, channeling scheme for judicial review of claims “arising from” removal proceedings, and § 1252(b)(9) in particular is designed to consolidate review into the petition-for-review process rather than permit collateral, systemwide APA suits in district court. Even if styled as prospective “access-to-process” challenges, respondents’ claims are tightly connected to the inspection, processing, and initiation of removal/asylum procedures at the border and therefore fall within the INA’s channeling and jurisdiction-stripping framework, which the APA cannot override. DHS v. Thuraissigiam confirms that noncitizens at the threshold have sharply limited judicial-review avenues beyond what Congress provided, and that federal courts should not expand review through constitutional or APA labeling where Congress has spoken. Given the institutional and workability concerns of allowing broad programmatic litigation to bypass § 1252’s scheme, I would hold jurisdiction lacking (or at least substantially limited) in district court.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252 establishes an exclusive review scheme that channels claims “arising from” the removal process into petitions for review and forecloses district-court jurisdiction “by any other provision of law,” including the APA. Under Jennings v. Rodriguez’s interpretation of § 1252(b)(9), the provision is broad but not limitless; here, however, respondents’ challenges to alleged border-processing practices are sufficiently connected to the initiation and conduct of removal/asylum screening to fall within Congress’s channeling design in §§ 1252(a)(5) and (b)(9). DHS v. Thuraissigiam reinforces that for noncitizens at or near the threshold, Congress may sharply limit judicial review to the narrow avenues it provided, and courts should not allow APA suits to functionally circumvent those limits. Because respondents’ requested prospective relief would effectively regulate how DHS processes would-be applicants in a context Congress placed within § 1252’s jurisdictional framework, the district court lacks jurisdiction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Sections 1252(a)(5) and 1252(b)(9) channel review of “order[s] of removal” and claims “arising from” removal proceedings into petitions for review, but (as construed in Jennings v. Rodriguez) they should not be read as a universal “zipper clause” that sweeps in independent, pre-removal challenges—here, alleged DHS policies and practices that prevent noncitizens from accessing the statutory asylum application process at or near ports of entry. Because respondents do not seek review of any particular removal order or the conduct of a completed removal proceeding, their APA and constitutional claims are best characterized as access-to-process challenges collateral to removal, not claims that must await a petition for review. Reading § 1252 to bar all such suits would risk serious constitutional concerns by leaving no meaningful forum to test systemic obstruction of congressionally created procedures, a concern that distinguishes this case from DHS v. Thuraissigiam, which addressed the narrow scope of habeas to attack an expedited removal order after an adjudication. Accordingly, the district court retains jurisdiction at least over these prospective, programmatic claims not inextricably linked to an individual removal order.
